## TL;DR

Updated the close-out guide to remove obsolete instructions for a fixed-name
`com.repoos.watchdog` LaunchAgent. The current implementation supports explicit,
per-repository background services managed by launchd or systemd, with OS-level
restart behavior and service health checks. No minute-by-minute standalone
watchdog or three-failure kickstart policy is present.

## Work and rationale

The task finding pointed to a statement in `docs/close-out-pipeline.md` that
described two global LaunchAgents: `com.repoos.serve` and
`com.repoos.watchdog`. It also told readers to bootstrap both plist files and
said the watchdog polled `/api/health` every minute, then kickstarted the service
after three failures. That guidance had become stale and could lead someone to
recreate an unsupported service setup.

I checked the surrounding guide, the current service manager, service routes,
and the completed service-management task (#0185). The implementation now
creates repository-specific service labels, offers launchd on macOS and a
systemd user unit on Linux, and keeps background service installation and
auto-start opt-in. Launchd's generated plist has `KeepAlive` rules for process
failure. RepoOS can explicitly check a service's health, and its stop/restart
handling accounts for replacement processes that the OS manager lost track of
after the reload handoff. There is no `com.repoos.watchdog` implementation or
periodic `/api/health` polling loop.

I replaced the obsolete A/B instructions with the supported foreground and
managed-service workflows. The guide now states that a foreground server is
started with `just serve`, while background operation is configured through
Settings or `repoos service`. It notes that these modes should not occupy the
same repository port simultaneously and links to the user-facing service
documentation. The dated 2026-08-23 crash-loop observation remains, but is
clearly marked as an earlier manual configuration rather than current setup.

## Approaches tried

I first searched for the exact watchdog label and related language across the
repository, then inspected the code paths that actually create service units
and perform service health checks. That showed the finding was valid as a claim
about the old fixed-name watchdog, while its suggested explanation was only
partly current: the new service manager does use OS-level restart behavior, but
it is per repository and paired with explicit controls rather than a separate
health-monitoring daemon. I therefore corrected the guide to describe the
implemented feature rather than merely changing the watchdog label.

## Challenges and blockers

The documentation mixes a historical development incident with instructions
that read as current operational guidance. Removing the entire incident would
discard useful context, while leaving the old commands would invite readers to
recreate stale LaunchAgents. I retained the incident with a short status note
that identifies its setup as obsolete. No implementation change was needed for
this documentation finding.

## Key learnings

The phrase “health watchdog” in the old task material refers to a design claim
that did not survive into the shipped service-management implementation. The
current distinction is between OS supervision of an opted-in service process
and RepoOS's explicit health-check action. Future operational docs should name
the service scope and trigger rather than carrying forward assumptions from an
earlier manual LaunchAgent setup.
